title: Work the Tolerance Boundary
skill: Reasoning at the edge of a rule
scenario: Clean invoices are easy. Today's four all land within a dollar or two of the band, where the larger-of rule earns its keep. One is rescued by the dollar floor even though it breaks the 2% leg; one sits exactly on the line; one is a hair over; and one on a big PO fails because the percentage leg, not the dollar floor, is now the larger number. Compute each and let the boundary decide.
input:
Tolerance band per invoice = the LARGER of 2% of the PO or 25.00; the boundary is inclusive (a variance equal to the band passes).
- INV-59101: invoice 1224.50 vs PO 1200.00. (2% of 1200 = 24.00, so the band is the larger of 24.00 and 25.00.)
- INV-59102: invoice 1225.00 vs PO 1200.00.
- INV-59103: invoice 1225.50 vs PO 1200.00.
- INV-59104: invoice 2045.00 vs PO 2000.00. (2% of 2000 = 40.00, so the band is the larger of 40.00 and 25.00.)
instructions: For each invoice compute variance = invoice total - PO total.
Compute variancePct = variance / PO total * 100, rounded to 2 decimals.
Set toleranceBand = the larger of 2% of the PO and 25.00 (25 for the 1200 POs, 40 for the 2000 PO).
Set withinTolerance true when variance is at or below the band - note INV-59101 passes on the 25 floor even though its percent is over 2%.
Return a JSON array of the four rows with numbers as numbers, then validate.
copilotPrompt: For four boundary invoices compute variance (invoice - PO), variancePct (variance / PO * 100 to 2 decimals), toleranceBand (larger of 2% of PO or 25), and withinTolerance (variance at or below the band, inclusive). Note INV-59101 passes on the 25 dollar floor despite being over 2%, and INV-59104 fails because on a 2000 PO the 2% leg (40) is the larger band. Return a JSON array with numbers.
successMessage: Boundary worked. INV-59101 rides the dollar floor, INV-59102 sits exactly on the line and passes, INV-59103 is a hair over, and INV-59104 fails on the percentage leg the larger PO exposes.
editorHelper: One row per boundary invoice - the larger-of rule decides.

intro.heading: Before you compute: the boundary is where the rule is real

sections.title: Larger-of has two legs, and either can win
sections.body: On a 1200 PO, 2% is 24.00, so the 25.00 dollar floor is larger and becomes the band. On a 2000 PO, 2% is 40.00, so the percentage is larger and becomes the band. The same rule produces a different band per invoice - you must compute which leg wins before you judge the variance.

sections.title: The dollar floor can rescue an over-2% variance
sections.body: INV-59101's variance is 24.50 - that is 2.04% of the PO, over the 2% leg. A percentage-only rule would reject it. But larger-of picks the 25.00 floor, and 24.50 is under 25.00, so it passes. This is exactly why the floor exists: to spare small benign gaps the percentage would wrongly catch.

sections.title: Inclusive means the line itself passes
sections.body: INV-59102's variance is exactly 25.00, equal to the band. The policy boundary is inclusive, so it passes - equal to the band is within the band. A rule that rejected the exact line would be arbitrary; being explicit about inclusive-or-exclusive is part of designing it.

sections.title: A larger PO changes which leg protects it
sections.body: INV-59104's 45.00 variance would pass under a flat 25 floor, but on a 2000 PO the 2% leg is 40.00 and wins the larger-of, so 45.00 is over. The percentage leg is what catches proportionally large overcharges the flat floor would miss.

takeaway.heading: You worked the rule where it bites
points: You computed the band per invoice instead of assuming one number - larger-of makes the band depend on the PO, and either leg can be the one that wins.
You saw the dollar floor rescue a variance that broke the 2% leg, and the percentage leg catch an overcharge the flat floor would have missed.
You treated the boundary as inclusive on purpose: a variance equal to the band passes, and that choice is part of the policy, not an accident.
Edge cases are where a rule is actually defined; anyone can classify an obvious pass or fail, but the boundary is the test of whether you understand the design.
The workflow can now be trusted at the margin, where sloppy tolerance logic quietly pays overcharges or rejects clean invoices.
